docs.title: Debrief v4
docs.text:
Debrief helps analysts turn the record of an exercise or deployment into understanding: reconstructing tracks, measuring geometry, annotating what happened, and producing reports whose every figure traces back to its data.

Debrief v4 replaces the 25-year-old Eclipse application with one shared core that every community uses: a VS Code extension, analysis tools written in Python, and plots stored as plain GeoJSON in STAC catalogues with their provenance inside.

  • Blog: short posts as each capability lands.
  • Guides: the style guide, interaction models and tool-author guide that keep Debrief consistent as it grows.

Development happens in the open at debrief/fuudee. Everything on this site uses unclassified sample data only.

docs.title: Blog
docs.text: Short, frequent posts on what is new in Debrief v4, written in the same pull request as the work they describe.

docs.title: How Debrief v4 fits together
docs.text:
Debrief v4 starts with foundations rather than features. Here is the shape everything else will hang from.

flowchart LR
    subgraph host["VS Code (or the web demo)"]
        ext["Debrief extension<br/>TypeScript"]
        views["Map, outline and tool panels<br/>webviews"]
        ext <--> views
    end

    subgraph python["Per-user Python services"]
        tools["Tool service<br/>MCP over REST"]
        kernel["Kernel<br/>time, units, geodesy, formatting"]
        tools --> kernel
    end

    subgraph disk["Your filesystem"]
        cat["STAC catalogue"]
        plot["Plots: GeoJSON<br/>with provenance inside"]
        src["Imported sources<br/>never modified"]
        cat --> plot
        cat --> src
    end

    schema["One schema in LinkML<br/>generates Python and TypeScript types"]

    ext -- "loopback only,<br/>per-session token" --> tools
    agent["AI agents"] -- MCP --> tools
    tools <--> cat
    ext <--> cat
    schema -.-> ext
    schema -.-> tools

A few choices shape everything:

  • Plots are plain files. A plot is a GeoJSON FeatureCollection, catalogued with STAC and carrying its own provenance. Anyone can read it without Debrief, and access control is simply the folder's permissions.
  • Analysis lives in Python. Every operation is a Python tool served over MCP, so the same tool serves the Debrief interface, an analyst's script and an AI agent. A scientist adds a tool by writing a Python file, without rebuilding Debrief.
  • One vocabulary. Every type that crosses between Python and TypeScript is generated from a single LinkML schema, so the two sides cannot drift apart.
  • Everything is recorded. Each change to a plot is recorded so it can be replayed, which is also how undo works.
  • The web demo runs the same tools. In the browser, the Python tools run under Pyodide; nothing is sent to a server.

The first foundations are in place: the schema and its generated types, and a kernel for time, units, geodesic measurement and display formatting. Three early checks came back positive. The schema approach works end to end; the Python code runs unchanged in the browser; and asking the Python service for each Tote update takes a few milliseconds, well inside the 100 ms an analyst needs to drag the time slider smoothly.

docs.title: Fast enough to drag
docs.text:
When you drag the time slider or a target solution, the numbers must keep up with your hand. We measured whether they will.

The Tote shows range and bearing to other platforms at the current time, and it must update within a tenth of a second of the slider moving. In Debrief v4 those numbers come from the Python service, one request per movement.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Analyst
    participant V as Debrief window
    participant P as Python service
    A->>V: drags time slider
    V->>P: Tote values at new time?
    P-->>V: ranges and bearings (about 2 ms)
    V-->>A: Tote updated
    Note over V,P: next request only once the last returns,<br/>always for the latest time

Each request took about 2 milliseconds, and never more than 7, even with twenty platforms: comfortably inside the tenth of a second.

Dragging a target motion analysis solution is harder, because every bearing in the period must be recomputed. With thousands of bearings, the straightforward code took a fifth of a second, too slow. Computing them all at once instead brought six hours of bearings at one a second down to under 40 milliseconds.

We measured on a development machine, so we will check again on an analyst's laptop before the target motion analysis work begins.

docs.title: Measuring on the real Earth
docs.text:
Debrief v4 measures ranges and bearings along the true shape of the Earth. Legacy Debrief did not, so some figures will change slightly.

Legacy Debrief treated each small patch of sea as flat, with one degree of arc equal to 60 nautical miles. Debrief v4 measures along geodesics on the WGS84 ellipsoid, the same model as GPS, whatever projection the map uses.

The difference is small but not zero. Worst cases, across every bearing:

Latitude Range Range differs by Bearing differs by 50° 1 nmi 7 m 0.09° 50° 10 nmi 70 m 0.16° 50° 50 nmi 350 m 0.5° 70° 50 nmi 430 m 1.1° 
flowchart LR
    old["Legacy: flat patches<br/>1° = 60 nmi"] -- "about 0.4% apart<br/>at UK latitudes" --> new["v4: WGS84 geodesics"]

If you compare a v4 figure with one from an old report, expect differences of this size. Bearing residuals in target motion analysis are the most sensitive: a solution built in legacy Debrief will not show exactly the same residuals in v4.

Every value shown on screen also goes through one formatting service, so knots, nautical miles, three-figure bearings such as 045.0°T, and Zulu times look the same everywhere.

docs.title: One schema, two languages
docs.text:
Debrief's analysis runs in Python and its interface in TypeScript. Every piece of data that passes between them is defined once, so the two sides cannot quietly disagree.

flowchart LR
    linkml["LinkML schema<br/>the one definition"]
    json["JSON Schema"]
    py["Python models"]
    ts["TypeScript types"]
    fixtures["Shared test files<br/>valid and broken examples"]

    linkml --> py
    linkml --> json
    json --> ts
    fixtures -. checked by .-> py
    fixtures -. checked by .-> ts

The schema describes plots, catalogues, the history of every change, tools and their parameters, and the analyst's display settings. From it we generate Python and TypeScript code; nobody writes those types by hand.

A few things we settled along the way:

  • Units travel with the numbers. A speed is stored as {"unit": "m/s", "values": [...]}, so a file can never leave you guessing. A speed labelled in degrees is rejected in both languages.
  • A plot is still plain GeoJSON. Positions stay as longitude and latitude in degrees, so any GIS tool can read a plot without Debrief.
  • The same examples test both sides. Over seventy example files, some valid and some deliberately broken, are checked by Python and by TypeScript. A plot written by one and read by the other comes back unchanged.

LinkML needed some help: its TypeScript output was unusable, and a few of its Python and JSON Schema outputs disagreed with each other. Each workaround now has an example file that would catch it coming back.

docs.title: Debrief's Python, in your browser
docs.text:
The public demonstration of Debrief will run its Python analysis tools inside your web browser. We checked that it works before building on it.

Pyodide is Python compiled to run in a browser. We ran the same test under ordinary Python and under Pyodide and compared every answer: geodesic measurements, closest approach, formatted values and over eighty example files.

flowchart LR
    test["Same test script"] --> cp["Ordinary Python"]
    test --> pyo["Python in the browser<br/>(Pyodide)"]
    cp --> cmp{"Identical?"}
    pyo --> cmp
    cmp -- yes --> ok["Pass"]

The answers were identical. Calculations run about half as fast in the browser, which is still far quicker than an analyst can notice, and the demonstration needs a few seconds to start.

This check now runs on every change. It also sets a rule for the future: any library a Debrief tool relies on must be able to run in the browser too, or the tool must say plainly that it is only available on the desktop.

Nothing in the demonstration leaves your browser, and it only ever holds unclassified sample data.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Three guides keep Debrief consistent as it grows one pull request at a time.

Guide North Star (draft) Owner All guides An analyst who has learned one part of Debrief can predict the rest. Style guide: language Say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon. Ian Mayo Style guide: theme and UI Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Ian Mayo Interaction models Predictable and forgiving: the same gesture does the same thing everywhere, and nothing is silent or irreversible (SUB-21, SUB-28). Ian Mayo Tool-author guide A scientist's first tool should take an afternoon. Ian Mayo

The North Stars are drafts for the team to refine during Phase 0. Owners are provisional until the team is staffed.

docs.title: How the guides grow
docs.text:
• A skeleton first. Each guide's version 0 names every top-level section, including empty ones marked with the phase that will fill them. New material goes into a known place. Material that fits nowhere is flagged at review as either new territory or out of scope.
  • With the feature. A guide is extended in the same pull request as the feature that needs it. The pull-request template asks.
  • Every entry cites what it serves. An entry cites the principle or requirement behind it (for example PRN-08 or CAP-24). An entry that cannot cite one is a warning sign.
  • Read end to end at every phase exit. Each owner reads their guide whole at the end of each phase, and resolves contradictions while they are few.

Automated checks for terminology and theme-token use arrive in Phase 1 (DEV-10).

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The terms Debrief uses in its interface, tools and documentation. The language section of the style guide says when to use them.

Adapted from DOMAIN_GLOSSARY.md in debrief/debrief-future, itself adapted from legacy Debrief's glossary, and corrected to the SRD. The changes are listed at the end.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Plot. The unit of analysis: one exercise serial or deployment period, its tracks, annotations, sensor observations and narrative, with the history of every change made to it. Stored as GeoJSON in a STAC catalogue (SUB-05).

Catalogue. A folder of plots, sources and supporting files, described in STAC. Each catalogue holds data of one protection level (SEC-02).

Source. A file imported into Debrief, such as a REP file or a legacy plot. Debrief never changes a source; a revision arrives as a new source (SUB-10).

Supporting file. Video, imagery, acoustic files and other content that is not geographic data, kept beside a plot (SUB-06).

History (in guides, provenance). The record of every operation that produced a plot: imports, tool runs, edits and deletions, with who or what made them (SUB-18 to SUB-24).

Fix. A single timestamped position of a platform, with course, speed and depth where known. Depth is positive down.

Track. The movement of one platform over time: its fixes in order.

Annotation. A shape, label, note or period of interest drawn on or attached to a plot (CAP-03). An annotation with only a time, such as a note or a period, has no position (CAP-04).

Named set. A saved selection of features, reusable as a selection or as a tool's input (TL-11).

Narrative. The log of events from each platform, imported from Word or PDF and combined on one time axis (CAP-19, CAP-20).

Serial. A period of an exercise, typically 4, 6, 12 or 24 hours.

docs.title: Sensors and TMA
docs.text:
Sensor. A device on a platform that observes others: sonar, radar or visual.

Sensor observations (contacts, cuts). Measurements from a sensor, in Debrief usually bearings. Weeks of them may be held as one set (CON-02).

Bearing. The direction from one position to another, measured clockwise from true north. A relative bearing is measured from the platform's own heading. Debrief displays true bearings as three figures: 045.0°T.

Ambiguous bearing. A towed-array bearing that could be on either side of the array: two candidate bearings mirrored about the array's axis. The analyst resolves each to one side (CAP-22).

Bearing error. The uncertainty of a bearing, where the sensor data supplies it. Debrief can draw such a bearing as a wedge of that width (CAP-22).

TMA (target motion analysis). Estimating a target's course and speed from bearings, typically bearing-only from passive sonar. A solution is rooted in a selected period of bearings, and its positions match the bearing times (CAP-21).

Residual. The difference between a measured bearing and the bearing to the solution at the same time. Small, unpatterned residuals suggest a good solution.

Leg. A period of steady conditions. An ownship leg has steady course and speed; a bearing leg has a steady bearing rate. Changes of ownship leg give the geometry TMA needs.

SATC (semi-automatic track construction). Generating a TMA solution automatically from bearings. Lower priority than manual TMA (CAP-21).

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Tote. The table of relative geometry between one primary and several secondary platforms at current time: range, bearing and other measures (CAP-06).

Measure group. A named, reusable set of measures for a mode of analysis, defined by a study's lead analyst. The Tote is a view onto one (CAP-07).

CPA (closest point of approach). The time and range at which two platforms are nearest.

Current time. The instant, within a time range, that every view follows. Shared state, with selection and viewport (SUB-26).

Display window. A period around current time outside which a layer's sensor data is hidden, so that weeks of bearings stay legible (CAP-28, CAP-29).

Storyboard. A sequence of map views, each with a time and narrative comments, exported as offline HTML, a PowerPoint quad chart or video (CAP-13, CAP-14).

Tool. An analysis operation written in Python: Debrief builds its form and offers it when it applies (section 6 of the SRD).

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Time. Stored in UTC to the millisecond (SUB-01) and shown in Zulu time unless the analyst chooses a display zone.

Position. Latitude, positive north, and longitude, positive east, on WGS84. Debrief measures range and bearing along geodesics on the WGS84 ellipsoid, whatever the map's projection (SUB-03). Legacy Debrief used a flat-earth model, so its figures can differ by about 0.4% in range.

Units. Every stored quantity carries its unit. Analysts choose display units: knots, nautical miles, yards, metres, kilometres, degrees (SUB-02, SUB-04).

Direction Degrees Radians North 0° 0 East 90° π/2 South 180° π West 270° 3π/2

docs.title: Changes from the earlier glossary
docs.text: Earlier glossary Now Why Times have microsecond precision Millisecond precision; finer legacy times are truncated on import and the truncation recorded SUB-01, EXT-14 Contacts carry frequency Frequency is not imported; acoustic analysis stays in the acoustic replay application CAP-22, EXT-03 Speeds include feet per second Knots, metres per second, kilometres per hour Schema unit enums Track segments: core, TMA, planning, infill Not yet in the v4 data model; TMA solutions are rooted in a bearing period CAP-21 Depth in every location Positions are latitude and longitude; a track may carry a depth series, positive down Schema 0.0.4 World Location, World Speed, World Distance, World Vector Position, quantities with units Implementation names, not domain terms Plot is a collection of tracks Plot is the unit of analysis, a GeoJSON FeatureCollection in a STAC catalogue SUB-05

docs.title: Interaction models
docs.text:
North Star: predictable and forgiving: the same gesture does the same thing everywhere, and nothing is silent or irreversible (SUB-21, SUB-28).

Worked patterns applied the same way across hosts, tools and agents (DEV-08). Each model is one short page: the requirements it cites, a Mermaid sequence diagram, and a pointer to its reference implementation. Where an interaction is already a requirement, the model cites it rather than restating it.

docs.title: Style guide
docs.text:
The style guide covers language, theme and user interface (DEV-07). It exists before the first webview or graphical feature, and pull-request review checks conformance to it (DEV-10).

Section North Star Status Language Say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon. Version 0 Theme Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Skeleton; filled from Phase 1 User interface Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Skeleton; filled from Phase 1

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
North Star: say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon.

Applies to every word a person reads: labels, messages, tool explanations (CAP-24), walkthroughs, blog posts and these guides. It builds on the glossary (DEV-07).

docs.title: Spelling and tone
docs.text:
• British English: colour, analyse, behaviour, centre, licence (noun), metres. Not "color", "analyze".
  • Plain and direct. Prefer the active voice and short sentences. Address the analyst as "you" in help and walkthroughs.
  • Sentence case for headings, labels and buttons: "Add annotation", not "Add Annotation".
  • Name things by what they are to an analyst, not how they are built (PRN-07, CAP-24).

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Use the glossary term. These replacements come up most often:

Write Not Why plot document, file, dataset A plot is the unit of analysis (SUB-05). track polyline, line feature fix point, record, row annotation shape, drawing, markup Shapes are one kind of annotation (CAP-03). catalogue repository, database, index The STAC catalogue (SUB-15); British spelling. source input file, raw file Imported sources are never modified (SUB-10). tool function, plugin, script history provenance log, audit trail In the interface. "Provenance" is fine in guides and the tool-author guide. undo to here revert, roll back Undo is replay to a point (SUB-21). current time playhead, cursor Shared state (SUB-26). bearing azimuth, heading Heading is the platform's own direction.

Abbreviations analysts already use (TMA, CPA, SATC, DR, OTG, DTG, AIS) need no expansion in the interface; expand them once in help text.

docs.title: Numbers, units and times
docs.text:
Display always goes through the formatting service (SUB-04), in Python or its TypeScript twin; never format a value any other way. Rounding is half away from zero. Its defaults are this guide's defaults:

Quantity Default Example Speed knots, one decimal 12.3 kn Range and distance nautical miles, two decimals 4.25 nmi Bearing three figures, true, one decimal 045.0°T Position degrees and decimal minutes 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W Time Zulu 09:30:05Z Date and time day month year, Zulu 11 Oct 2026 09:30:05Z Date-time group military DTG 110930Z OCT 26 Local time, if chosen offset from UTC 10:30:05 UTC+1
  • Put a space between a number and its unit (12.3 kn), but none before °.
  • Times are Zulu unless the analyst chose a display zone, which is shown as an offset from UTC (10:30:05 UTC+1), never an abbreviation such as BST. Never write a time without its zone.
  • Use the analyst's chosen units everywhere, including in tool explanations: write "the window, in the units you have chosen", not "the window in metres".

docs.title: Tool-author guide
docs.text:
North Star: a scientist's first tool should take an afternoon.

For scientists writing their own analysis tools (DEV-09, OUT-06). A tool is a Python file: it declares what it applies to and what parameters it needs, and Debrief builds its form and offers it when it applies, without being rebuilt (TL-05, NFR-08).

Drafted in Phase 1 from the team's experience writing the first tools, and tested by a scientist building a real tool in Phase 5. It will cover:

  • Tool declarations (TL-04, TL-06): name, explanation, the feature kinds the tool applies to, its parameters and its outputs. The schema already defines these; see schemas/linkml/tools.yaml.
  • Debrief data types (TL-09): tracks, annotations, sensor observations, quantities with units.
  • User-facing explanations (CAP-24), following the language section of the style guide.
  • Results (TL-11): new features, changes, non-spatial results and named sets.
  • Randomness and replay (SUB-20): declare it, and Debrief records the seed.
  • Running in the browser (CON-09): use pure-Python libraries, or ones in Pyodide.
